With either type of surficial geology, elevation is an important dimension of drainage. High grounds have an advantage over low grounds since water stagnation and the danger of spot floods, during periods of high precipitation, are minimized. In most cases, modern technology can overcome the shortcomings of low grounds.
The terrain in the study area is mostly gray clayey and silty clayey till, relatively low in content of pebbles, cobbles, and boulders. It contains local lenses of silt, commonly mantled with 1 to 2 feet of leached silt and clay.
I. Existing and Proposed Land Use
Present urban development along Lincoln Highway includes residential areas, retail stores, service industries, automobile-oriented businesses and vacant land. The four communities served by this section of Lincoln Highway each have land use maps prepared by planning consultants, although the plans have not been officially accepted by the communities. These plans, however, are in general use and with few exceptions the land use patterns proposed by the planners are developing on the ground. A composite land use is shown in Exhibit "7". (This exhibit is only for general informational purposes to indicate how collected data was visually displayed and related to the proposed improvement at the public hearing. Due to budgetary and manpower restraints, the Illinois Department of Transportation does not have the capability of reproducing good land use exhibits for the Negative Declaration.)
Much of the property along Lincoln Highway is, or will be, part of a strip development, at least one block deep, primarily involved in automobile-oriented or other highway businesses, interlaced with retail stores. Those residential areas in Chicago Heights that front on Lincoln Highway can be expected to become business properties within the lifetime of this improvement. The residential property in Park Forest, however, should retain its present classification as the property faces away from the highway. The undeveloped land in Olympia Fields which lies between the Illinois Central Railroad and Western Avenue, also is developing with residential lots facing away from the highway and should keep this portion of Lincoln Highway residential in nature.
That portion of Olympia Fields west of the Illinois Central Railroad already is developing as a highway-oriented business district.
It probably will continue to develop that way on the north side
of Lincoln Highway from Olympian Way west to the western side of
Evergreen Street where, again, residential property faces away
from the highway.
